awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: CIRC: Planning-C: O-Milli-RAN - An O-RAN-compliant, Softwarized mmWave Radio Stack with Flexible PHY and MAC
awd_abstract_narration:
This planning project will engage the Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE) community on millimeter-wave (mmWave) and advanced wireless research to gather feedback and gauge support for a new research infrastructure that introduces the principles of open, disaggregated, and “softwarized” radio access networks to mmWave systems. This planning project will analyze research priorities, platforms, and interfaces to inform the development of an experimental research infrastructure combining flexible radio capabilities and control loops based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) within mmWave systems. The intent is to enable adaptive wireless experimentation over high-frequency systems, offering new opportunities for creating, training, evaluating, and improving mmWave systems on realistic, over-the-air scenarios. The goal of this planning effort is to (1) understand the needs of the CISE community; (2) scope enabling technologies and architectural building blocks; and (3) lay out the design for an adaptive mmWave system that would spur experimental research and development exploring high-frequency bands for 6G and beyond.  

This planning project will provide an initial assessment of the need and potential for an adaptive mmWave research infrastructure, adopting the principles of open and softwarized radio access networks to mmWave systems. The planning activities involve (1) mapping and interviewing relevant stakeholders, including members and officers of the O-RAN Alliance, the Next G Alliance, and PAWR (Platform for Advanced Wireless Research) facilities; (2) conducting community surveys across academic, industry, and government participants to understand their research priorities, needs, and pain points; and (3) visiting existing wireless testbeds to gather insights into their capabilities and limitations, as well as to identify enabling technologies and architectural building blocks. This project will co-design the research vision and infrastructure architecture with the CISE research community and contribute back by disseminating its findings, potential use cases, and designs to help support and motivate additional research and important standardization and regulatory decisions related to high-frequency bands for 6G and beyond.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Project Outcomes Report

The major goal of this planning project was to engage the CISE research community and industry stakeholders to assess the support, needs, and priorities for creating O-Milli-RAN, a one-of-its-kind, O-RAN–compliant, softwarized mmWave (and FR3) radio stack with flexible PHY and MAC layers. The envisioned platform aims to enable experimental research on high-frequency radio access networks (RANs) by leveraging principles of openness, programmability, and AI-native control loops available in O-RAN. Such an infrastructure would open vast opportunities for CISE researchers to design, test, and refine adaptive PHY and MAC solutions in realistic over-the-air environments.

Major Activities and Objectives

To achieve this vision, the project carried out three core activities:

  1. Stakeholder Engagement:
    • Mapped out the research and industry stakeholder landscape.
    • Identified and interviewed 14 stakeholders spanning academia, testbed operators, startups, and major vendors across three continents.
    • Collected insights on community needs, research priorities, and limitations of existing testbeds.
  2. Technology Scoping:
    • Assessed the current state of hardware and software platforms for high-frequency research.
    • Identified gaps, including the lack of support for low-latency radio control and flexible PHY/MAC programmability.
    • Conducted site visits to Rutgers University and Arizona State University to study their testbeds and ongoing experimental research.
  3. Community Survey Development:
    • Designed a comprehensive survey grounded in the insights from interviews and scoping activities.
    • The survey evaluates research priorities, target use cases, technical gaps, and familiarity with enabling technologies.
    • This survey will provide quantitative evidence to inform the co-design of O-Milli-RAN.

The specific objective of these activities was to gather both qualitative and quantitative evidence to assess the feasibility, community support, and value proposition of developing O-Milli-RAN.

Significant Results and Key Outcomes

Through interviews and site visits, several key outcomes emerged:

  • Community Support: There is strong interest from both academia and industry in advancing experimental research on high-frequency bands, particularly for testing AI-driven, adaptive PHY and MAC solutions within O-RAN.
  • Expansion Beyond FR2: While the original focus was on mmWave bands in FR2 (24–60 GHz), stakeholder feedback revealed growing demand for research infrastructure in FR3 (6–24 GHz). As a result, the project vision expanded to cover FR3 as well, reflecting shared technical characteristics with FR2 and emerging research needs.
  • Identified Gaps: Stakeholders emphasized the lack of existing platforms that support low-latency, fine-grained control of radios in high-frequency bands. This confirmed the unique value proposition of O-Milli-RAN.
  • Technology Mapping: The team identified open-source and commercial technologies that could serve as building blocks for the envisioned stack, while also recognizing critical gaps requiring new development.
  • Knowledge Base: The project generated hours of recorded stakeholder interviews, which will be made available after project completion to inform the broader research community.

Together, these activities validated the need for a programmable, O-RAN–compliant research infrastructure for high-frequency RAN experimentation and helped refine its design scope.

Training and Professional Development

The project created valuable training opportunities for early-career researchers and students. Participants included two faculty members (one young tenure-track professor), one postdoctoral researcher, and multiple graduate and undergraduate students. They gained hands-on experience in:

  • Conducting professional interviews with leading stakeholders in academia and industry.
  • Exploring mmWave hardware and O-RAN software for preliminary experiments.
  • Understanding the end-to-end process of research infrastructure planning and technology scoping.

This exposure provided students and junior researchers with skills in technical engagement, community building, and cross-disciplinary collaboration.

Next Steps

During the next reporting period, the project team plans to:

  1. Define Research Vision and Architecture: Synthesize inputs from interviews, site visits, and surveys to articulate a clear research vision, high-level system architecture, and value proposition for O-Milli-RAN.
  2. Identify Funding Opportunities: Explore alternative funding pathways given changes to the NSF CIRC program, including opportunities with federal agencies, state initiatives, and industry partners.
  3. Disseminate Findings: Extend and adapt the community survey and stakeholder engagement outputs to support alternative funding proposals and collaborations.

Overall Impact

This planning grant successfully engaged a diverse set of stakeholders, identified critical technology gaps, and built consensus around the need for an open, softwarized research infrastructure for high-frequency O-RAN experimentation. By expanding its scope to include both FR2 and FR3, the project adapted to community needs and positioned O-Milli-RAN as a transformative platform that can drive innovation in adaptive PHY/MAC design, AI-native RAN control, and experimental wireless networking research.
